item.title: Making Federal Climate Policy Work — Wed Nov 11, 12:00 PM — None
item.description:
Students, faculty and staff are invited to attend the first Nicholas Institute and UPEP Environmental Institutions Seminar Series presentation of the fall 2026 semester. The speaker will be David Vogel, Professor Emeritus, University of California, Berkeley, and coauthor of the recently published When Federal Climate Policy Works: Benefits, Business, and Politics. This is an in-person event with no virtual viewing option; no registration required.
During Vogel's talk, he will describe and explain the effective climate policy accomplishments of the federal government in six policy areas: appliance energy efficiency standards, automotive fuel-economy standards, the promotion of renewable energy, restrictions on chemicals that function as GHGs, and restrictions on methane emissions from landfills and oil and natural gas production. Understanding what distinguishes these policy accomplishments from the better-known federal policy failures offers important lessons for the political future

Two key themes are increasing the expressive capacity of the environmental models used in SLAM systems (representation) and improving the performance of the algorithms used to estimate these models from data (inference). item.title: In-Context Learning with Applications in Healthcare and Clinical Research — Wed Nov 11, 2:00 PM — None
item.description:
Abstract: In-context learning refers to the capacity of large language models to perform a new task based solely on a small number of examples or instructions provided within the prompt, without any retraining. This capability is particularly valuable in healthcare, where labeled data are scarce, difficult to obtain and privacy constraints are substantial. Given only a few illustrative examples, a model can identify events (clinical trial endpoints) from medical histories, estimate risk for the occurrence of future events, or assess patient eligibility for clinical trials. A single model may therefore be adapted efficiently to a range of tasks and revised as clinical guidelines evolve, provided that its outputs are rigorously validated and remain subject to expert oversight.

item.title: Physics Colloquium - Angular momentum transport in magnetic insulators - a probe of quantum magnetism — Wed Nov 11, 3:30 PM — None
item.description: Magnetic interactions allow emergent collective excitations like magnons (quantized spin waves) to transport electronic angular momentum even in insulators, when charge degrees of freedom are localized. In recent years, electrical techniques based on the spin Hall effect and its inverse have made it possible to examine the excitation and propagation of spin angular momentum in magnetic insulators. This opens up new avenues for studying insulating quantum magnets, systems in which strong magnetic interactions and geometric frustration lead to competing ordered states and quantum fluctuations. Of particular interest are candidate quantum spin liquids, in which quantum fluctuations are theorized to prevent long-range order and lead to exotic fractionalized spin -carrying excitations. I will introduce the ideas and techniques, and I will show recent experimental results on thermally driven spin transport in a transition metal oxide and a Kitaev-like quantum magnet, finishing with an outloo

item.title: Book Talk: Liberation is Other People — Wed Nov 11, 5:00 PM — East Duke Parlors
item.description:
Join us for a book talk and Q&A with author Dr. Alexis Shotwell.
"Liberation Is Other People" begins with the truth that many of the crises we face-climate collapse, war, systemic inequality-are human-made and therefore humanly transformable. Yet such complex problems cannot be solved by heroic individuals working incredibly hard, or being personally pure and upstanding. Every attempt to repair exposes how deeply our lives are entangled across histories of power, privilege, and vulnerability. Rejecting the idea that personal virtue or guilt can solve the world's problems, Alexis Shotwell offers a philosophy and practice of collective freedom through collective struggle. Drawing on thinkers such as Angela Davis and Ursula K. Le Guin, she argues that freedom is not the power to act alone but the capacity to shape the world with others. item.title: The Influenza Paradox: When Biomarkers Mislead and Models Reveal the Biology — Thu Nov 12, 10:00 AM — None
item.description:
Abstract: Advances in high-throughput technologies have dramatically increased our ability to characterize disease, yet understanding the mechanisms underlying disease progression well enough to predict clinical outcomes remains a major challenge. This seminar will describe how mechanistic mathematical models integrated with multimodal data can infer hidden biological processes, explain why similar biomarker profiles can arise from fundamentally different disease states, and improve predictions of disease outcomes. Using influenza as an example, I will illustrate how this framework reveals mechanisms that are inaccessible to direct measurement and provides a foundation for predictive, mechanism-based precision medicine.

item.title: Degrees of Aging: Education and the Unequal Biological Risk in Later Life — Thu Nov 12, 12:00 PM — SSRI-Gross Hall 270
item.description: Abstract: Biological-aging measures summarize physiological functioning across bodily systems and offer a way to examine how social inequality becomes embodied. This talk synthesizes four studies using biomarker data from the Health and Retirement Study and National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. The studies document racial and ethnic differences in biological aging partly associated with childhood socioeconomic conditions and education; widening educational inequality despite overall population improvements; economic, social, psychological, and behavioral pathways linking education to biological aging; and racial, ethnic, and nativity differences in the predictors and health consequences of accelerated aging. Together, the findings demonstrate that population averages can conceal widening inequality and substantial heterogeneity in how social conditions shape physiological functioning. item.description:
PineCone’s Old Time Jam takes place on the 2nd Thursday of each month from 7-9 p.m. at Riparian Provision Company (1408 South Saunders Street, Raleigh). This is an up-to-speed, gather-in-a-circle kind of jam. It’s led by great players who work to make sure there’s space for everyone in the tunes.
The leader picks a key (D, A and G are popular) and calls tunes in that key until it feels right to pick a new key and retune. The fiddlers traditionally call the tunes, but they’re not always the jam leader. If you’re playing fiddle you should expect to be asked, “Hey, you got a good D tune?” While “no” is an acceptable answer, it’s good to have a tune in each key that you’d feel comfortable calling and kicking off.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Tue Feb 9 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.
Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. Duke offers locations where faculty, staff and students can receive a free flu vaccination. Vaccinations can also be obtained at Duke Primary Care providers, area pharmacies and other locations, but documentation must be provided for compliance.
Annual vaccination against the flu is a condition of employment at Duke Health; other University staff and faculty working on-site must be vaccinated or have an approved medical or religious exemption to maintain access to Duke's buildings and facilities.
Find out more at vaccines.duke.edu.
Source: Duke University
